title: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP IN FRONT OF ISRAEL—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THIS STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE HE EVER CLIMBED THOSE STAIRS
paragraphs: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP IN FRONT OF ISRAEL—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THIS STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE HE EVER CLIMBED THOSE STAIRS

2 Samuel 16:21–22 | A son publicly humiliates his father. A family collapses beneath the weight of hidden sin. A kingdom watches in disbelief. And behind one of the darkest scandals in Israel’s history stands a warning about unforgiveness, the consequences of sin, and the desperate need for a Savior who can redeem what human rebellion has destroyed.
There are some Bible stories that make you close the book for a moment.
Not because you doubt God.
But because you cannot believe what human beings are capable of doing to one another.
A son climbs onto the roof of his father’s palace.
Below him is Jerusalem.
The city that once celebrated his father’s victories. The city where worship rose toward heaven. The city where a shepherd boy who had once faced Goliath became the king of Israel.
And now that king is running for his life.
Not from the Philistines.
Not from a foreign army.
From his own son.
And what Absalom is about to do on that rooftop is so deliberately humiliating, so calculated, and so morally devastating that Scripture refuses to soften it.
Listen to the words of 2 Samuel 16:21–22 in the King James Version:

“And Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
Read that last sentence again.
“In the sight of all Israel.”
This was not a private romance.
This was not a misunderstood family dispute.
This was an act of sexual exploitation, political domination, and public humiliation.
Absalom was announcing to the nation that he had taken his father's throne, his household, and his royal authority.
And the women caught in the middle?
They were treated as instruments in a man's war for power.
The Bible does not tell us that they freely consented. We must not pretend that it does. Nor should we turn their suffering into sensational entertainment.
These women were human beings.
They had names, histories, fears, and dignity, even though this passage does not preserve their individual voices.
And there is something deeply disturbing about a society in which powerful men can use vulnerable people to prove who is in control.
But here is the question that should trouble every person reading this.
How does a son become so consumed by bitterness that he is willing to destroy his own father's dignity before an entire nation?
Because Absalom did not wake up one morning and suddenly become this man.
There was a history.
There were wounds.
There was blood.
There was silence.
And there was sin that nobody could undo.
To understand that rooftop, we have to go backward.
Back to another rooftop.
Back to David.
Years earlier, King David had walked upon the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba bathing.
Second Samuel 11 tells us that David sent for her, took her, and slept with her. Bathsheba was married to Uriah, one of David's soldiers.
David then attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his attempts failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in deadly combat and abandoned.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
And for a moment, perhaps from the outside, it appeared that the king had managed to bury the scandal.
But the final verse of 2 Samuel 11 declares:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
Those words should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because people can applaud what God condemns.
People can overlook what God sees.
People can be impressed by someone's position while remaining completely unaware of the corruption taking place behind closed doors.
David was Israel's king.
He was also a sinner who had grievously abused his power.
And no crown, calling, anointing, ministry, or spiritual reputation could make that evil righteous.
God sent the prophet Nathan to confront him.
Nathan announced consequences that would reach into David's own household.
In 2 Samuel 12:11–12, the Lord declared that calamity would arise against David from within his house and that what David had done secretly would be answered by public humiliation.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 contains a devastating contrast:
בַסָּתֶר — bassāter, meaning “in secret.”
And:
נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — neged kol-Yisra'el, meaning “before all Israel.”
David had tried to conceal his wrongdoing.
But its consequences would become publicly visible.
This does not mean that God approved of Absalom's later actions. God's judgment upon David never turned Absalom's wickedness into righteousness.
It means that the Lord had warned David that his sin would bring consequences far beyond the moment in which he committed it.
And that is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
But forgiveness does not always erase the earthly consequences of what we have done.
A marriage may be forgiven and still require years of rebuilding trust.
A child may forgive a parent and still carry painful memories.
A leader may genuinely repent and still need to surrender a position of authority.
David confessed his sin.
Psalm 51 reveals the language of a broken man pleading for mercy:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
And Nathan assured David that the Lord had put away his sin.
But David's household was not suddenly healed.
There is a difference between receiving God's forgiveness and escaping every consequence of our choices.
Then another terrible event unfolded.
David's son Amnon violated his half-sister Tamar.
Second Samuel 13 records the violence, the shame, and Tamar's devastation.
And Absalom, Tamar's brother, knew what had happened.
Scripture says David became very angry.
But the biblical account does not record David administering justice to Amnon.
Imagine the pain inside that household.
Tamar had suffered a terrible wrong.
Amnon remained alive.
David was angry.
And Absalom watched.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of pain.
Not the details of this royal family.
But the experience of seeing wrongdoing go unaddressed.
Watching someone powerful avoid accountability.
Hearing people tell the wounded to move on while the person responsible never seems to face the truth.
Maybe you have sat at a family gathering where everyone pretended nothing happened.
Maybe you learned to smile while carrying a memory nobody wanted to discuss.
Maybe the person who should have protected you remained silent.
If that is part of your story, hear this clearly.
What happened to you was not made acceptable by someone else's silence.
And God does not require you to call evil good.
Absalom's grief and anger over Tamar's suffering were rooted in a genuine injustice.
But what he eventually chose to do with that anger became another tragedy.
Second Samuel 13:22 says:
“And Absalom spake unto his brother Amnon neither good nor bad: for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.”
There is something chilling about those words.
Neither good nor bad.
Silence.
Not reconciliation.
Not peace.
Not justice.
Silence.
For two years, Absalom waited.
Then he arranged for Amnon to be killed.
The brother who had violated Tamar was dead.
But murder did not restore Tamar.
It did not heal the family.
It did not bring Absalom peace.
Instead, Absalom fled.
Years passed.

He eventually returned to Jerusalem, but his relationship with David remained fractured. When David finally received him and kissed him, the outward gesture did not mean every underlying wound had been resolved.
And eventually, Absalom began stealing the hearts of Israel.
He stood near the city gate.
He listened to people's grievances.
He presented himself as the leader who would give them justice.
He cultivated loyalty.
He built influence.
He prepared rebellion.
And eventually, he declared himself king.
The wounded son had become a calculating political rival.
That is one of the most sobering movements in this entire narrative.
Absalom had witnessed injustice.
Then he committed injustice.
He had seen the damage caused by the misuse of power.
Then he used power to harm others.
He had watched his family fracture.
Then he helped tear the kingdom apart.
His pain was real.
But his pain did not justify his cruelty.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because some of us have been hurt so deeply that we are tempted to believe our suffering gives us permission to hurt someone else.
We think, After what they did to me, they deserve whatever happens.
We think, They made me this way.
We think, I am only giving them back what they gave me.
But vengeance does not become holy because the wound behind it is genuine.
Romans 12:19 tells believers not to take vengeance into their own hands.
That does not mean ignoring abuse, avoiding lawful accountability, or pretending that injustice is harmless.
It means refusing to make personal revenge our god.
And now we arrive at that rooftop.
David has fled Jerusalem.
Absalom has entered the city.
His adviser Ahithophel proposes a public act designed to make reconciliation with David politically impossible.
The concubines David left to care for the palace are still there.
In the ancient royal world, taking possession of a king's women could function as a claim to his royal prerogatives.
This is part of the political meaning of Ahithophel's advice.
But there is another detail that should not be overlooked.
In the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:22, the phrase translated “in the sight of all Israel” is:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'enei kol-Yisra'el.
Literally, “before the eyes of all Israel.”
This is the language of public visibility.
The narrative describes a tent being erected on the roof and Absalom going in to his father's concubines.

It does not require us to imagine that every citizen literally witnessed the sexual act itself. The point is that the act was made publicly known and carried out as an unmistakable political declaration.
The rooftop had become a stage.
The women had become victims of a struggle for power.
The son had made himself his father's enemy.
And the nation was being forced to witness the consequences of a collapsing royal household.
Now notice the terrible connection.
David's earlier sin involving Bathsheba began with what he saw from a palace rooftop.
Absalom's public humiliation of David took place on a palace rooftop.
The two scenes are not identical, and the victims must never be treated as interchangeable.
But the narrative echoes are difficult to miss.
The king who once abused his power now suffers humiliation at the hands of a son who is abusing his own.
Sin has consequences that can spread through households and communities.
Yet we must be careful here.
The Bible does not teach that every child is destined to repeat a parent's sins.
It does not teach that a victim of family dysfunction is doomed to become an abuser.
And it does not teach that someone else's wrongdoing removes our personal responsibility.
Ezekiel 18:20 makes that clear:
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.”
David was accountable for David's sin.
Absalom was accountable for Absalom's sin.
And the women harmed by their actions were not responsible for the evil done against them.
This is not a story about an unavoidable family curse.
It is a story about real human choices, real moral responsibility, and devastating consequences.
And perhaps that is what makes it so frightening.
Because somewhere in this story, we may recognize something about ourselves.
Not necessarily in the sexual scandal.
Not necessarily in the political rebellion.
But in the resentment.
The pride.
The secrecy.
The desire to control.
The temptation to punish someone who wounded us.
The desperate effort to make sure nobody ever humiliates us again.
You can carry bitterness so long that it begins to feel like your personality.
You can rehearse an injury so often that revenge starts sounding like justice.
You can become so determined never to be powerless again that you begin controlling everyone around you.
And you can look spiritually respectable while your heart is slowly hardening.
That is why Hebrews 12:15 warns about a “root of bitterness” that springs up and troubles many.
Notice that.
Many.
Bitterness rarely stays confined to the person carrying it.
It affects marriages.
Children.
Friendships.
Churches.
Communities.
Sometimes the people who suffer most from our unhealed anger are people who never caused the original wound.
And still, we have to make another distinction.
Healing is not the same as forced reconciliation.
Forgiveness does not mean giving an unsafe person unrestricted access to your life.
Repentance does not mean avoiding accountability.
Biblical grace never requires us to deny the truth.
The Gospel calls us away from vengeance while also calling evil what it is.
And this is where the story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Absalom's rebellion eventually ends in his death.
Second Samuel 18 records that he was caught in a tree during battle and killed by Joab and his men, despite David's instruction to deal gently with him.
When David heard the news, the king was overcome with grief.
He cried:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” — 2 Samuel 18:33, KJV
Think about that cry.
The father whose throne had been stolen.
The father whose household had been publicly humiliated.
The father whose son had sought his downfall.
He is not celebrating.
He is weeping.
And suddenly the story is no longer merely about a scandal on a rooftop.
It is about a father grieving a son who will never come home.
There will be no final conversation.
No opportunity to confront everything that happened.
No reconciliation scene.
No embrace after the rebellion.
Absalom is dead.
And David is crying for him.
We must not romanticize their relationship or pretend David was an innocent father who did everything right.
He did not.
But neither should we ignore the anguish of this moment.
David's lament reveals the unbearable grief of a father facing the death of his son.
And those words—
“Would God I had died for thee”—
lead us toward a greater question.
What if there were a King who did not merely wish to die for His enemies?
What if there were a King who actually did?
This is where we must turn from David's broken household to Jesus Christ.
Not because Absalom's wickedness secretly becomes good.
Not because the abuse of vulnerable women was necessary for salvation.
Not because every disturbing biblical event is a hidden symbol of Jesus.
But because the failure of Israel's kings exposes the desperate need for a King who is truly righteous.
David was anointed, but he was not sinless.
Absalom was admired, but he was not righteous.
The throne of Israel could not save its people from the corruption of the human heart.
And then, generations later, Jesus came.
The promised Son of David.
The Messiah.
The King whose kingdom would not be established through sexual exploitation, murder, manipulation, or the humiliation of the powerless.
Jesus did not seize a throne by trampling on the vulnerable.
He came to serve.
He did not cover His own sin.
He had no sin to cover.
He did not sacrifice innocent people to preserve His power.
He offered Himself to save guilty sinners.
Listen to the contrast.
Absalom sought power by publicly shaming his father.
Jesus submitted to public shame in obedience to His Father.
Absalom's rebellion led to death.
Christ's obedience led through death to resurrection and life.
Absalom sought a kingdom through treachery.
Jesus established His kingdom through righteousness, sacrificial love, and victory over sin and death.
Philippians 2:8 declares:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
And Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
In the Greek text, the expression is:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν — eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn.
“While we were still sinners.”
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not after we had become spiritually impressive.
Not after we had managed to hide all our failures.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
And it is not cheap grace.
It cost the Son of God His life.
On the cross, Jesus bore the judgment due to sinners, and through His resurrection He conquered death.
He did not die so we could continue celebrating rebellion.
He died to reconcile us to God and free us from sin's dominion.
This is why repentance matters.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of a change of mind or heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is not crying because our reputation was damaged.
It is not asking God to remove consequences while refusing to abandon the behavior that caused them.
True repentance acknowledges sin, turns toward God, and bears fruit consistent with that turning.
And that may be the most uncomfortable part of this article.
Because perhaps the greatest danger in your life right now is not a public scandal.
Perhaps it is a private compromise.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A lie you keep defending.
A relationship you keep using for selfish purposes.
A secret habit you keep excusing.
A person you refuse to forgive, even as you acknowledge that forgiveness may require boundaries rather than restored closeness.
Or perhaps you are the one carrying the wounds of someone else's wrongdoing.
You have been living with shame that should never have been placed upon you.
You have wondered whether God saw what happened.
Whether He cared.
Whether the silence of others meant heaven was silent too.
Please hear this.
Jesus sees the wounded as well as the guilty.
He does not confuse the victim with the perpetrator.
He does not demand that the abused carry the blame of the abuser.
He does not call darkness light.
And His compassion is not reserved for the people who appear strong.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
You may need the courage to repent.
Or you may need the courage to stop blaming yourself for someone else's sin.
You may need to confess.
Or you may need to seek safety, wise counsel, and support.
You may need to release vengeance.
Or you may need to pursue justice without surrendering your heart to hatred.
The Lord knows the difference.
And His Word is capable of reaching places that religious appearances never touch.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not merely a slogan.
But understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the evil never happened.
He does not turn sin into innocence through denial.
He does not promise that every earthly relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
He rewrites lives by forgiving repentant sinners, making the spiritually dead alive, giving the wounded hope, and forming a new people through His Gospel.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not that every memory disappears.
It is that union with Christ brings a new identity and a new life.
Your past does not have to be your master.
Your worst decision does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your family's history does not have to dictate your future.
And the wound someone inflicted upon you does not have the authority to determine your worth before God.
Jesus Christ is greater than your shame.
His mercy is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
And His resurrection is the declaration that death does not have the final word.
If this story has exposed something you have been carrying, do not rush away from that conviction.
Ask yourself what you have been doing with your pain.
Have you brought it to Christ?
Or have you allowed it to become the reason you keep wounding others?
Have you mistaken silence for peace?
Have you mistaken revenge for healing?
Have you mistaken public religious activity for private surrender?
And if you have been hurt by someone who should have protected you, have you begun believing the lie that their wrongdoing somehow diminished your value?
You are not worthless because someone treated you without dignity.
You are a human being made in the image of God.
And Christ's invitation to come to Him is not restricted to people whose stories are clean.
There is room at the foot of the cross for the ashamed.
For the grieving.
For the guilty who repent.
For the exhausted who need rest.
For those who are finally ready to stop pretending.
If you want to respond to the Lord today, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, You know the parts of my story that I have hidden from others. You know where I have sinned, where I have been wounded, and where bitterness has taken root. Forgive my sins. Teach me to repent without excuses and to receive Your grace without pride. Help me pursue truth, justice, and healing without becoming consumed by revenge. Protect those who are vulnerable. Give me courage to make right what I can, accept accountability where I must, and entrust what I cannot control to You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Lead me into a life that honors You. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if you prayed that sincerely, do not let the moment end with emotion alone.
Open your Bible.
Seek a faithful, Christ-centered church.
Learn to follow Jesus in the ordinary decisions of everyday life.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Practice truth even when nobody is watching.
The Gospel is not merely a powerful feeling during a difficult story.
It is the good news of Jesus Christ that calls us into a transformed life.
If this article touched a wound you have been carrying, or confronted a bitterness you have struggled to surrender, consider leaving a comment.
You can write “Christ is still healing me” if you are trusting Him through a difficult season.
You can write “No more hiding” if you are ready to bring a hidden struggle into the light.
You do not have to share private details or expose someone else's story. A few honest words can be enough to let other believers know they are not alone.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus delivered you from bitterness, restored your faith, or taught you to forgive without abandoning wisdom and healthy boundaries, your testimony may encourage someone who has almost given up.
There is another way you can help this message reach people who may never enter a church building.
Not because God measures your love by an algorithm.
But because someone in your circle may be carrying a wound that this Scripture speaks to.
Someone may be trapped in resentment.
Someone may be quietly excusing a destructive sin.
Someone may believe their past is too shameful for the mercy of Christ.
And a message about repentance, grace, and the saving power of Jesus may be exactly what they need to encounter.
Because spiritual growth rarely happens through one emotional moment.
It happens as we continue abiding in Christ and allowing His Word to shape us.
That is also why we are building and expanding Gospel Warrior.
We want biblical teaching and spiritual nourishment to remain accessible to people who cannot afford expensive resources.
For some believers, regular financial support of a Gospel ministry is a meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship.

Scripture encourages believers to support Gospel work. First Corinthians 9:14 speaks of those who proclaim the Gospel receiving their living from the Gospel, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure or compulsion.
That distinction is important.
You can honor Christ through prayer, faithful service, generosity, sharing biblical truth, and countless acts of obedience.
These items are simply resources and reminders. They are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
The Word of God is.
The souls of people who need biblical truth are.
And now, return in your mind to that rooftop in Jerusalem.
A son is claiming a kingdom through humiliation.
A father is fleeing the consequences of a broken household.
Vulnerable women are caught in the violence of powerful men.
A nation is watching.
And a terrible chain of human choices is unfolding.
There is no reason to celebrate that scene.
It is tragic.
But the Bible does not leave us with Absalom as our hope.
It leads us beyond the failures of earthly kings to the righteous Son of David.
To Jesus.
The King who did not come to exploit the helpless, but to rescue sinners.
The King who did not need to conceal His wrongdoing, because He had none.
The King who accepted a crown of thorns before receiving the glory of His exaltation.
The King who was publicly mocked, crucified, buried, and raised again.
And that King is still calling people to repent and believe the Gospel.
Not tomorrow, when the consequences become unbearable.
Not someday, when the bitterness has consumed another generation.
Today.
While there is still time to tell the truth.
Still time to seek forgiveness.
Still time to turn away from sin.
Still time to trust the Savior.
Because the greatest tragedy is not merely that Absalom died in rebellion.
It is that so many people today continue living in rebellion while the mercy of Christ is being proclaimed to them.
Do not let your pain become your throne.
Do not let your shame become your identity.
Do not let your sin become your refuge.
Bring everything into the light of Jesus Christ.
The rooftop revealed what sin can destroy, but the cross reveals what only Jesus can redeem.
